clue.text: Back in a mo

blocks.note: first meaning: to support
a very short moment of time

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a note pinned to a door; 'Back' is a verb meaning support, and 'a mo' is a brief instant.
explanation.definitionFit: To second a proposal is to support it, and a second is also the tiny unit of time a 'mo' suggests.

clue.text: David for example embodies resistance as moral greatness

indicators.note: to embody is to contain within a body, so the first word holds the next

blocks.note: R is the symbol for electrical resistance
Michelangelo's David is a famous sculpture

explanation.surface: Michelangelo's David is held up as an emblem of resisting, a model of virtue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'David' suggests the biblical king, but it is the statue.
explanation.definitionFit: Stature means standing or reputation earned by achievement or character, as well as physical height.

clue.text: A capital city without one b….. tree

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the letter for one is dropped from the city

blocks.note: the capital of Egypt
I is the Roman numeral for one
the letter itself, trailing off as if a word is censored

explanation.surface: A capital lacks even one blasted tree.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots make 'b' look like a censored swear word, but it is just the letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The carob is a Mediterranean evergreen tree whose pods are used as a chocolate substitute.

clue.text: Disregard information about the French court

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the word for information is read backwards

blocks.note: gen is British slang for information
the French masculine article
CT is the abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: Ignore what you hear about a French court case.
explanation.walkthrough: Gen is British slang for information.
explanation.definitionFit: To neglect something is to fail to pay it attention, which is to ignore or overlook it.

clue.text: Computer literacy primarily gets Pat new work

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter of the word before is kept
something made new is remade, so the name before it is rearranged into a fresh order

blocks.note: the first letter of literacy
the name rearranged
OP is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: Someone called Pat is given a new job because of good computer literacy.
explanation.definitionFit: A laptop is a portable personal computer small enough to rest on the knees.

clue.text: Wily like the earliest Native American people

indicators.note: earliest marks the first letter of the word next to it

blocks.note: as can mean like
the first letter of the
the Ute are a Native American people of Utah and Colorado

explanation.surface: Someone cunning, like the first inhabitants of America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Earliest' seems to describe the people, but it takes just the first letter of 'the'.
explanation.definitionFit: Astute means shrewd and quick to see an advantage, close to cunning or crafty.

clue.text: Managed against the odds to board wrong troopship

indicators.note: to board a ship is to get on and be inside it, so the first pieces go inside

blocks.note: to run something is to manage it
SP, starting price, is a bookmaker's odds
a tort is a civil wrong in law

explanation.surface: Someone managed, against the odds, to get onto the wrong troop vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Against the odds' reads as one idiom; 'against' only sets the managing next to SP, the starting price in betting.
explanation.definitionFit: A transport is a ship carrying troops or stores, so it names a military vessel.

clue.text: Stop by before five to get English books

blocks.note: pre- is a prefix meaning before
V is the Roman numeral for five
E is short for English
NT, the New Testament, is a set of books

explanation.surface: Drop in before five o'clock to collect some English books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stop by' reads as one phrasal verb meaning visit; the definition is 'Stop' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: To prevent something is to stop it from happening or to keep it from going ahead.

clue.text: Kind of dented the rear somehow

indicators.note: somehow signals the letters reach the result by some unexplained rearrangement

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone sort of bashed in the back of a car in an unclear way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kind of' reads as 'sort of'; split it, and 'Kind' is the definition with 'of' joining.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone tender-hearted is compassionate and easily moved to sympathy, which is being kind.

clue.text: Just as likely

blocks.note: first meaning: even-handed, equitable
second meaning: promising

explanation.walkthrough: 'Just as likely' reads as one phrase about equal odds; split it, and 'Just' and 'likely' are separate meanings joined by 'as'.
explanation.definitionFit: A just ruling is an equitable one, and an older sense of the word means promising or with good prospects.

clue.text: Fellow having energy to put on course for dogs

indicators.note: to be put on a course is to be placed within it, so the course's letters surround the fellow

blocks.note: a common man's name
E is the symbol for energy
Greats is the Oxford degree course in classics

explanation.surface: A man with plenty of vigour is sent on a training course.
explanation.walkthrough: Greats is the informal name for the Oxford University classics course, which a solver outside Britain may not know.
explanation.definitionFit: Great Danes are a breed of very large dog, so the plural phrase names several of these hounds.

clue.text: Fight for control over central Zambia

indicators.note: central asks for the letters at the very centre of the country's name
the word for control sits over and around the next piece, enclosing it

blocks.note: to rule is to control
the middle two letters of this six-letter name

explanation.surface: A power struggle breaks out for control of the heart of Zambia.
explanation.walkthrough: Zambia has six letters, so its centre is two letters, not one.
explanation.definitionFit: A rumble is slang for a street fight or brawl between gangs.

clue.text: Couldn’t stand trial after returning newspaper boss starts to expose duplicity

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the boss's short title is read from right to left
starts asks for the opening letter of each of the following words

blocks.note: ED is short for editor
a trial is a test
the first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: An editor can't bear a court case brought after a scoop exposing someone's double-dealing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' just places the trial after the reversed editor; the order of pieces follows the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: If you could not stand someone, you loathed them, so the past tense verb for hating fits exactly.

clue.text: It offers a better chance of success being the boss’s moll

definitions.text: It offers a better chance of success

blocks.note: the head is the boss, here in the possessive
a moll is a gangster's girlfriend, loosely a tart

explanation.surface: Being the gangland chief's girlfriend gives you an advantage in life.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as HEAD'S TART, the boss's moll; a moll is a gangster's female companion.
explanation.definitionFit: A head start is an advantage given or gained at the outset, improving one's odds of winning.

clue.text: Princess’s irritability caused by disease

blocks.note: Di, Princess Diana, in the possessive
a temper is a fit of irritability

explanation.surface: A princess's bad moods are blamed on an illness.
explanation.walkthrough: Di is Princess Diana, a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Distemper is a viral illness of dogs and other animals, so it is a kind of disease.

clue.text: Ginsberg perhaps cut lines from verse

indicators.note: cut means removed, so the lines are taken away from the word for verse
from shows which word the lines are taken out of

blocks.note: RY, railway, is the usual shorthand for lines
verse is poetry

explanation.surface: Allen Ginsberg trimmed some lines from one of his poems.
explanation.walkthrough: Lines means railway lines, abbreviated RY, not lines of a poem.
explanation.definitionFit: Allen Ginsberg was a Beat writer of verse such as Howl, an example of the category.

clue.text: Indifferent therefore to the truth

blocks.note: so can mean therefore
so can mean true, as in 'is that so?'

explanation.surface: Someone is therefore unconcerned about whether things are true.
explanation.definitionFit: Indifferent here means mediocre, neither good nor bad, which is the sense of the reduplicated phrase.

clue.text: Go on about current thing Button wants to avoid

indicators.note: about means around, so the first word wraps around the next

blocks.note: in means fashionable, current
to spout is to go on talking at length

explanation.surface: Someone harps on about electrical current and a button to be avoided.
explanation.walkthrough: Button is Jenson Button, the British Formula One world champion, not a switch beside the current.
explanation.definitionFit: A spin-out is a car skidding off track, an accident any racing driver tries hard to avoid.

clue.text: Was economical over gallery floor

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the verb before it is read backwards

blocks.note: to save is to be economical
the Tate is a London gallery

explanation.surface: Someone cut costs on the flooring of an art gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Floor' looks like a noun in a building but is a verb meaning knock flat; the Tate is a famous London gallery.
explanation.definitionFit: To floor someone is to overwhelm or shatter them, which is what devastating news does.

clue.text: Maybe Peter‘s pet also strayed

indicators.note: to stray is to wander off course, so the letters drift out of order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Peter's pet wandered off as well.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s after Peter stands for 'is', joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter was one of the twelve disciples of Jesus, so he is an example of the group.

clue.text: This mountain feature is hard to spot

blocks.note: a tarn is a small mountain lake
taken as written
H is short for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: This feature of the mountains is difficult to see.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard to spot' reads as difficult to see, but 'spot' is the definition, a verb meaning stain.
explanation.definitionFit: To tarnish is to stain or sully, just as to spot something is to mark or blemish it.

clue.text: Put up with enclosing the end of Porthmeor beach

indicators.note: enclosing means surrounding, so the word for put up with wraps around the letter
the end asks for the final letter of the place name

blocks.note: to stand something is to tolerate it
the last letter of Porthmeor

explanation.surface: Tolerate the far end of Porthmeor beach, in St Ives, Cornwall.
explanation.walkthrough: Porthmeor is a surfing beach in St Ives, Cornwall; here only its last letter matters.
explanation.definitionFit: A strand is a literary word for a shore or the land along the edge of the sea.

clue.text: Fictional vet is far from first-class

indicators.note: fictional means made up, so the letters that follow are invented into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A vet in a novel turns out to be far from top-notch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Far from first-class' suggests a poor rating, but 'from' only links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Five-star is the top rating for hotels and the like, so it describes something of the highest quality.

clue.text: Cross on account of splitting extremely old shoe

indicators.note: splitting means cutting into, so the first pieces go inside and divide the outer one
extremely means at the extremes, so only the end letters of the word are used

blocks.note: X is a cross
for can mean because of
the first and last letters of old

explanation.surface: Someone is cross because an old shoe has split.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' reads as angry, but it is the letter X.
explanation.definitionFit: An oxford is a type of laced leather shoe, a specific example of footwear.

clue.text: Fine to embrace Liberal’s intuitive discernment

indicators.note: to embrace is to hug, so the first word wraps its arms around the letter

blocks.note: fair weather is fine weather
L is short for Liberal

explanation.surface: It is fine to welcome a Liberal politician's gut instinct.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s after Liberal stands for 'is', joining wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Flair is a natural aptitude or instinctive feel for doing something well, a kind of innate judgment.

clue.text: Smug politician interrupting to cancel review

indicators.note: to review something is to go over and rework it, so the letters are rearranged
to interrupt is to break into, so the politician sits inside the other letters

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
an MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A self-satisfied politician butts in to scrap a review.
explanation.definitionFit: Complacent means self-satisfied and untroubled by possible shortcomings, the same attitude as being smug.

clue.text: Even parts of Bambi have it to some extent

indicators.note: even parts are the letters in second and fourth places, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: the second and fourth letters of the name
taken as written

explanation.surface: Bits of the film Bambi contain something special to a degree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Have it' looks like one phrase, but 'have' just joins; only Bambi's even letters are taken.
explanation.definitionFit: A bit is an informal phrase meaning slightly or somewhat, to a modest degree.

clue.text: A string of invectives from head of institute in Deal

indicators.note: the head is the top, so the first letter of the following word is taken
in places the single letter inside the word for deal

blocks.note: the first letter of institute
to deal is to trade

explanation.surface: An institute head in the Kent town of Deal unleashes a stream of abuse.
explanation.walkthrough: Deal is a seaside town in Kent, but here it means trade.
explanation.definitionFit: A tirade is a long, angry speech of criticism, which is a stream of abusive invective.

clue.text: Want to be right in the end

indicators.note: in places the single letter inside the word for the end

blocks.note: R is short for right
death is the end of life

explanation.surface: Someone longs to be proved right in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Want' reads as a verb meaning desire, but it is a noun meaning lack.
explanation.definitionFit: Want in the sense of lack or scarcity is exactly what a dearth is: a shortage of something.
